mechaber.1#main: The law how we nullify with sixty. In it are 2 seifim: A piece that absorbed an issur and does not have sixty in it to nullify it — if it fell into a pot — it does not forbid except according to the calculation of the issur in it; that is, if in what is in the pot there is, together with the piece itself, sixty against the issur absorbed in it — what is in the pot is permitted; but the piece itself is forbidden, because the issur in it does not fully leave from it (Rashba and Tosafot chapter 3, daf 100, and Rosh and Mordechai there and Semag daf 50b and Sefer HaTerumah siman 52 and so in the language of R' Efrayim himself in the novelae of Rashba daf 110 and at the end of Sefer Raavan and so Maharshal chapter 3 siman 57 and all the Acharonim) (and so is primary (Gra, Kereti) and not like what was written above siman 92 that even that piece is permitted) — which is not so in a thing that was mixed and dissolved, that if blood or the like fell into permitted gravy and they were forbidden because of its minority and afterward the permitted gravy increased until there is sixty in all of it to nullify the blood — all is permitted, because everything was mixed and intermingled: {Rama: And according to what we practice saying in all issurim "a piece becomes nevelah" — there is no distinction between a moist thing and a dry thing except for this matter; that if what became forbidden was already a dry thing and there is sixty against it — the piece that was first forbidden remains in its prohibition and must be removed from there if one recognizes it; and if one does not recognize it — it is nullified if it is not a piece worthy of honor (Shach, Gra); and if it is a moist thing — everything is permitted once there is sixty against what was first forbidden; and see above siman 92 and 99.}
mechaber.2#main: A piece that has milk in it that was cooked in a pot that has sixty to nullify the milk — one must be careful not to remove anything from the pot while the forbidden piece is still inside, lest it remain at the end when there is no sixty in the pot to nullify the milk; and likewise one should not remove it first, because the milk in it will forbid it — what is its remedy? Leave it until the pot cools: {Rama: And according to what is established for us that "a piece becomes nevelah" — one removes the forbidden piece from there and the rest is permitted (logical opinion).}

mechaber.1#main: The law of one who cooks eggs and a repulsive thing found in a dish. In it are 2 seifim: One who cooks many eggs in their shells — he should not remove them from the water in which they were cooked until they have cooled, or he should put cold water on them to cool them, and afterward remove them — lest we fear that he will find an embryo in one of them; and if he were removing from them before they cooled — perhaps the one that has an embryo in it would remain with the last ones and would forbid them, because there would no longer be sixty there to nullify it: {Rama: And if he did not do so but poured them into a bowl and one of them was found to be tereifah — some forbid everything, lest the tereifah remained at the end and there was not sixty in the pot to nullify and what is in the pot became forbidden and in turn forbids everything in the bowl (Beit Yosef in name of Semag and Arukh); and likewise small fish in which an impure fish was found in the bowl if he did not pour them all at once into the bowl — then there is concern lest the issur remained at the end (Taz); and some permit in every case (Tur in name of Yesh Omrim) — for we do not establish an issur to say the issur remained without sixty (Beit Yosef in name of R"SH); and so is primary; and even according to those who forbid — one need not forbid the vessels in which it was cooked (Beit Yosef in name of Semag and Hagahot Maimoniyot) — for we maintain the vessel on its presumption.}
mechaber.2#main: A fly and the like among repulsive things that a person's soul recoils from — that was found in a dish — one throws them out and the dish is permitted, for emission from these spoiled things does not forbid (and see s.k. 6): {Rama: And so is the widespread custom even though some are stringent — the words of the lenient are primary (Beit Yosef ruled like Rashba and Rokeach and Tur siman 104); and one should not change the custom; and if he took with the spoon an impure fish from the pot or another thing that does not spoil — forbidden to return the spoon to the pot (Gra); and if he returned it — need sixty from the pot against the issur, not against the whole spoon (logical opinion — for we do not say regarding a vessel "a piece becomes nevelah"); but if there was a little of the dish with the issur on the spoon and it was returned to the pot — need sixty also against the little dish, for the piece became nevelah on the spoon (Arukh general rule 27).}

mechaber.1#main: Not to bake heter and issur in one oven. In it are 7 seifim: One may not roast kosher meat with nevelah meat or meat of an impure animal in one oven, and even though they do not touch one another; and if he roasted them — behold it is permitted, and even if the forbidden was of a large species and the permitted thin; and if the oven is large — that holds twelve se'ahs and its mouth is open — permitted to roast them in it, provided they do not touch one another; and if one of them is covered in a bowl or in dough or the like — permitted to roast them even in a small oven with a closed mouth: {Rama: And the same law applies to meat with milk (Tur siman 97); and the custom is to be stringent l'chatchila even in a large oven, and b'dieved to be lenient even in a small oven (Arukh general rule 39 unlike Beit Yosef and in responsum of R' Yosef Mintz and Hagahot ShaDa and Agur in name of Maharil and Tur in name of Rashba that so agreed most poskim and it is the view of Rashi and Hagahot and Rif and Rambam); and if he baked bread with meat — forbidden to eat it with milk if he has other bread (there); and likewise if a gentile baked bread with issur — forbidden to buy that bread if there is other bread, for all this is called l'chatchila; but if he has no other bread in abundance — permitted in both, for this is called b'dieved for this matter (Agur in name of R' Yosef Molin); some say one does not permit reicha even b'dieved unless the oven is open a little on the side or above where the smoke exits (there in Arukh); and in a place of loss one need not be stringent b'dieved (as it appears from the poskim and so Beit Yosef) even if completely closed; and if the issur is a sharp thing — and all the more if the heter is a sharp thing — reicha is significant (Taz, Kereti) and even b'dieved forbidden if both are uncovered; but if one of them is covered — even merely in dough — permitted (Mordechai chapter 3 and Or Zarua); if they baked or roasted issur and heter under one uncovered pan — forbidden (Tosafot) even b'dieved (there in Arukh); and the same if they baked in such a case bread with meat — forbidden to eat it with milk (ShaDa siman 60 and Maharai); but one after the other there is no concern (responsum of Maharam end Laws of Forbidden Foods and responsum of R' Yosef and Or Zarua) unless the pan sweated from both — then forbidden even one after the other if both were uncovered, for it is like covering of a pot (logical opinion from implication of Rosh siman 93) as above siman 93; some say wherever we say reicha is significant and forbids b'dieved — that is specifically when there is not sixty of heter against the issur; but when there is sixty of heter — even everything in the oven nullifies the issur (there in Arukh general rule 39 seif 18); and for need of loss one may practice thus. Some say an issur that forbids in any amount such as chametz on Pesach — reicha is significant and forbids even b'dieved if the oven is small and closed and issur and heter are uncovered in the oven (logical opinion in name of Hagahot Semak and in name of Tosafot Avodah Zarah daf 66b); and some say there is no distinction (logical opinion in name of Mordechai); and in a place of loss one may rely on the lenient; and see below end siman 118 whether to be stringent l'chatchila to place two pots, one of them of issur, on the stove, or to roast issur next to heter.}
mechaber.2#main: In what case is this said — in roasting; but if he comes to cook them in a pot — each for itself — even in a small oven with a closed mouth it is permitted, and even though the mouths of the pots are uncovered: {Rama: And specifically when the oven is open a little; but if it is closed on all sides as is customary to insulate hot food for Shabbat need — forbidden (Mahariu siman 44 and Or Zarua and Hagahot ShaDa in name of Maharam); and even b'dieved some are stringent and forbid if issur and heter are uncovered (as appears in Hagahot ShaDa); and in a place of great loss one may be lenient.}
mechaber.3#main: If there is grease of issur on the spit called paleh — forbidden to place heter on it all day; however when it is not within its day — permitted to use it, because it is possible in another manner: {Rama: As long as it is within its day hagalah does not help on it, nor peeling in a craftsman's vessel (Terumat HaDeshen siman 130 and Hagahot ShaDa and Mordechai).}
mechaber.4#main: Hot bread placed on top of an open barrel of libation wine — forbidden (and specifically if placed against the bung) (Arukh general rule 39); but if the bread is cold — permitted, even if the barrel is open; or hot bread and the barrel is bunged (meaning sealed) — permitted; and if it was barley bread — forbidden if the bread is hot, even if the barrel is bunged.
mechaber.5#main: Permitted to smell in one's mouth the scent of libation wine through the hole in the barrel to know if it is good: {Rama: But forbidden to taste it even though one does not swallow it (Ribash siman 288); and forbidden to sprinkle libation wine that is forbidden in benefit (in Sha'arim in name of Hagahot Ashiri end Avodah Zarah); but permitted to sprinkle their ordinary wine, for it is permitted in benefit (Arukh general rule 39).}
mechaber.6#main: A sack of pepper and ginger that they place in jugs of libation wine — permitted to smell them; but for spices of Havdalah — forbidden.
mechaber.7#main: Spices of idolatry and kilayim of the vineyard and orlah — forbidden to smell them.

mechaber.1#main: The law of dry in dry that became mixed. In it are 2 seifim: A piece that is not worthy of honor that became mixed with others — same kind, dry in dry (meaning that it is not blended and the issur stands by itself but became mixed and one does not recognize it) (Beit Yosef in name of responsum of Rashba and Ramban and Sefer HaTerumah) — one in two is nullified and permitted to eat them, one person each one by itself; but he may not eat all three together; and there is one who forbids one person to eat them even one after another: {Rama: And so one should practice l'chatchila; and some are stringent to throw one out or give to a gentile (Hagahot ShaDa in name of Maharam and Rashi in Avodah Zarah daf 74a); and this is only a general stringency; and all this is when mixed in its kind; but when not in its kind and one does not recognize it — even dry in dry — need sixty (Tur in name of Baal HaTerumah and many other poskim); and there is no distinction in all this whether the issur is d'rabbanan or d'oraisa (Beit Yosef in name of poskim unlike Hagahot ShaDa); and see above siman 122 if vessels became mixed together.}
mechaber.2#main: Dry in dry that was nullified one in two — if they cooked them all as one, and even to eat each one by itself — forbidden if there is not sixty, because the gravy is noten ta'am and is absorbed in the pieces; and if he wants to cook them together and there is not sixty — permitted to increase upon them so that there is a measure of sixty and to cook them, and there is no concern of nullifying issur: {Rama: And some say if the mixture was known before they were cooked together — all is permitted, for they do not return and become forbidden after they were nullified dry (Tur in name of Rosh and R' Yerucham in name of Tosafot, and he wrote that so is primary); and in a place of loss one may rely on the lenient and permit.}

mechaber.1#main: The law of safek treifot that occurred in meat. In it are 10 seifim: An important thing forbids in its kind in any amount; and they are seven things, and these are: peeled nuts and Badan pomegranates and sealed barrels and turnip stalks and cabbage heads and Greek gourd and loaves of the master of the house; and likewise important animals are not nullified; but other things — even though their way is to count them — behold these are measured by their measure: {Rama: And some say that every davar sheb'minyan — meaning whose way is always to count it — is not nullified (Tur in name of R"I and Beit Yosef); and so is the custom. That an important thing is not nullified is only d'rabbanan, and we follow its doubt leniently (Arukh general rule 25 and Rambam chapter 17 of Forbidden Foods and Tosafot Zevachim end daf 73 and Agudah there and Rosh chapter 3 and Rashba in Teshuvot and Nimukey Yosef chapter HaAreil and many other poskim as will be explained in this siman in several places):} Every thing that is important to the people of a place among the places — such as peeled nuts and Badan pomegranates in Eretz Yisrael in those times — forbids in any amount according to its importance in that place and at that time; and these were mentioned only because they forbid in any amount in every place; and the same applies to everything similar to them in other places.
mechaber.2#main: Animals that became mixed with others and were slaughtered — their importance is nullified and they are nullified — and that is when they were slaughtered b'shogeg (and specifically small animals that are not worthy of honor after their slaughter) (Or Zarua general rule 25).
mechaber.3#main: Nine stores sell slaughtered meat and one sells nevelah meat, and one took from one of them and it is not known from which of them he took — behold this is forbidden, for every fixed case is considered half-and-half; but meat found in the market or in the hand of a gentile — permitted, since most stores sell slaughtered meat, for "whatever separates from the majority separates" — this is Torah law; but the Sages forbade it even though all the slaughterers and all the sellers are Jewish: {Rama: And see above siman 63; and that which we say "whatever separates from the majority separates" — that is when it did not separate before us; but if it separated before us, or one sees when the gentile took it — it is as if he took it from there in his hand (Tur in name of Rashba and Tosafot chapter 3 daf 95 and Ran there and Hagahot Orach Chaim in name of R"I and Tosafot and Agudah chapter HaTaarovot and Rosh in responsum general rule 20 siman 15 and Semag end daf 52 and Semak siman 214 and ShaDa siman 46 and R' Yerucham net 15 and Maggid Mishneh chapter 5 of Forbidden Foods in name of the commentators).}
mechaber.4#main: A majority of stores sell slaughtered meat and a minority sell nevelah meat; one took from one of them and does not know from which he took, and it became mixed with others and is not recognizable — nullified in the majority because of a double safek: {Rama: And some forbid in such a case, because wherever the issur is in its place it is considered half-and-half, and since the first safek is forbidden by Torah law there is no further safek here to permit — only mixtures are not called a double safek (Arukh general rule 25) — and so is the custom.}
mechaber.5#main: One who took meat from the slaughterhouses (meaning the butcher shops) — and even a piece worthy of honor — and a treifah was found in the slaughterhouses and the treifah pieces were not known and he does not know from which he took — all that they took from the slaughterhouses before the treifah was found is permitted, for the safek did not fall in a fixed case but only after it separated; and since the majority is kosher — permitted; but what he took from then on is forbidden, and even a piece not worthy of honor — for not everyone is expert in this and they err between worthy of honor and not worthy of honor.
mechaber.6#main: Animals and other important things that became mixed in heter that are not nullified even in a thousand — even if one of the majority separated after the mixture became known — forbidden; and that is when he separated them intentionally; but if it separated by itself — permitted: {Rama: And that which it is forbidden if he separated them intentionally — that is when he separated only a little and some of the issurim remained in their place, for then we fear lest he also take from the fixed quantity; but if all of them separated together and none remained in their place, and at the time of their removal some of those that separated — then those that separated are permitted (words received from his father-in-law the Gaon Mahar"R Shachna z"l); only the last two are forbidden (Tur end siman 57); and if a treifah chicken became mixed with kosher ones and an egg was found among them — the egg is permitted, even though chickens are important and are not nullified regarding an egg — we follow the majority (Arukh general rule 26).}
mechaber.7#main: A thing that is not nullified because of its importance, such as animals and beriah and a piece worthy of honor, and a thing that has matirin that became mixed with others and one of them was eaten b'shogeg (whether he himself ate b'shogeg or others ate him b'shogeg) (Terumat HaDeshen siman 175) (Kereti) or it fell by itself into the sea in a manner that it is lost from the world — the others are permitted, for we attribute to say the issur went away; and specifically when eating the remainder two by two together, for from your soul there is one that is permitted; but to eat them one by one — forbidden: {Rama: And even to eat them two by two — forbidden for one person to eat all of them; and even two people may not eat all of them at once (Beit Yosef per view of Tur).}
mechaber.8#main: A thing that is not nullified because of its importance that became mixed with others and one fell from this mixture to two others and one fell from the three to two others — behold these others are permitted, for behold the one of the first mixture was nullified in the majority; and if one of the first mixture fell into a thousand — all are forbidden, and we do not say nullified in the majority except to permit their double safek — that if it falls from the second mixture to another place it does not forbid. (Language of Rambam chapter 16 of Forbidden Foods law 9): {Rama: And in any case one person may not eat all of them; and specifically when the issur that became mixed is a definite issur; but a safek issur that became mixed and fell from that mixture to another place — the second mixture is permitted (Arukh general rule 26); some say a thing that has matirin one may not permit through double safek (there general rule 25) — and it is good to be stringent if not for need, since he has a permit in any case.}
mechaber.9#main: Safek treifah that became mixed with others — all are forbidden until there is in the heter enough to nullify the issur, if it is among things that are nullified; since the first safek was in its body — one may not permit it through double safek: {Rama: And some say the reason it is forbidden is because the safek (Taz) is a d'oraisa issur and we cannot say another safek that there is no issur here only that it became mixed with others — is not called double safek and is forbidden (there); but if there were two doubts whether there was any issur here at all (Gra, Baer Hetev, Kereti) and both doubts became known together — they permit double safek in every place even in d'oraisa issur and the body of the issur; and even if it had a presumption of issur, such as a chicken standing in a presumption of issur and its wing broke or fell off — safek whether from life or after slaughter; and if you say from life — perhaps the lung was not perforated (Taz) — one may permit through double safek (Gra) even though one could clarify through examination of the lung — one need not be concerned (Taz, Baer Hetev); and see above siman 53.}
mechaber.10#main: A treifah lung that was found among kosher lungs and the examiner said he knew that adhesion and by mistake that treifah lung became mixed among the kosher ones, and it was not a random mixture of sheep — the sheep are permitted.

mechaber.1#main: The law of pots of tereifah meat that became mixed with kosher ones. In it are 7 seifim: Two pots — one of heter and one of issur — and before him two pieces, one of heter and one of issur; if the piece is from a d'rabbanan issur, such as the fat of the gid hanasheh, and these fell into each other — they are permitted, for we suspend judgment to say the issur fell into the issur and the heter into the heter; and even if the heter in the pot is not greater than what is before him; and the same law applies if there was only one pot of slaughtered meat and one of these two pieces fell into it and it is not known which it is — we suspend judgment that the heter piece fell, even if the heter is not greater than the issur; or if there was only one piece of d'rabbanan issur and there are two pots, one of heter and one of issur, and it is not known into which it fell — in this too we suspend judgment to be lenient.
mechaber.2#main: In what case is this stated — that we suspend judgment in all these to be lenient even if the heter is not greater than the issur — when the issur is also not greater than the heter; but if the issur is greater than the heter we do not suspend judgment to be lenient.
mechaber.3#main: If the issur was from the Torah we do not suspend judgment to be lenient to say it fell into the issur until the heter is greater than the issur so that it will be nullified within it by Torah law.
mechaber.4#main: If the heter was greater than the issur so that it would be nullified within it by Torah law — we suspend judgment to be lenient. How so? Two pots — one of slaughtered meat and one of nevelah — and a piece of nevelah fell into one of them; if the heter in the pot of heter is slightly greater than the piece of nevelah we suspend judgment to be lenient, because by Torah law species in its species is nullified in the majority, except that the Sages required sixty. If the two pots were of one species and the issur of another species we do not suspend judgment to be lenient until the heter is sixty times the issur.
mechaber.5#main: If there were two pots of heter and before them two pieces, one of heter and one of issur, and one fell into this one and one into that one — both are forbidden, even in d'rabbanan issur, if neither has enough to nullify the issur; but if one of them has enough to nullify the issur — both are permitted.
mechaber.6#main: If there were two pots of heter and issur fell into one of them and it is known into which it fell, and again issur fell into one of them and it is not known into which — I say that to the place of the first issur the second also fell; but if issur fell into one of them and it is not known into which, and afterward issur fell into one of them and it is known into which — both are forbidden: {Rama: And specifically when there is not sixty to nullify the issur that fell there; but if there was sixty to nullify the issur that fell there it is as if no issur fell there at all (Beit Yosef in name of Rashba).}
mechaber.7#main: If there were two pots of heter and issur fell into one of them and it is not known into which, and one does not have enough to nullify the issur but both together have enough to nullify it — both combine to nullify it; and not only that but even one in the house and one in the attic combine; and the same law applies even for a hundred. In what case? When all belong to one person, for whatever belongs to one person will eventually become mixed; but if they belong to two people they do not combine: {Rama: And some are stringent that even for one person one may not be lenient; and for need of loss one may permit for one person; however one may not eat it except after they have been mixed together, for then the issur has already been nullified (Arukh general rule 26 in name of Maharish).}

mechaber.1#main: The laws of tevilat kelim (immersion of vessels). In it are 16 seifim: One who buys from a non-Jew eating vessels of metal or of glass, or vessels coated with lead on the inside — even though they are new — must immerse them in a mikveh or a spring of forty se'ah (Tur in the name of Sefer HaMitzvot and Avi Ezri): {Rama: Some say that vessels coated with lead, even on the inside, one immerses without a blessing (Beit Yosef in the name of Semak and Arukh) — and so is the practice.}
mechaber.2#main: The vessel must be loose in his hand at the time of immersion, for if he grips it tightly in his hand it is a chatzitzah (interposition); and if he moistened his hand in water first — there is no concern. (And specifically if he moistened his hands in mikveh water, but not in drawn water) (it appears from Mordechai, chapter HaSocher).
mechaber.3#main: He recites a blessing on immersion of a vessel; and if they are two or more he recites a blessing on immersion of vessels.
mechaber.4#main: Tripods upon which pots are set do not require immersion; but plates require immersion because the food itself is placed upon them.
mechaber.5#main: A slaughtering knife (or a knife used for skinning) (Arukh) — some say it does not require immersion: {Rama: And some disagree (Teshuvot Beit Yosef) and it is good to immerse it without a blessing; the iron tools with which matzot are made do not require immersion (Arukh); and likewise a cover that is pressed onto dough to bake it; but a pot cover requires immersion (Hagahot Ashiri).}
mechaber.6#main: A wooden vessel that has iron hoops on the outside that support it does not require immersion.
mechaber.7#main: A silver cup attached to a wooden vessel requires immersion: {Rama: And likewise a pepper mill within wood that has fixed iron with which one grinds requires immersion (Mordechai); and likewise iron funnels or iron spigots and all other metals — all require immersion (Arukh); and specifically when the main vessel is of metal; but if the main vessel is of wood and only a little fixed iron is in it — since it is possible to use it without the iron — it does not require immersion; but a vessel fixed with iron pegs without which it would not be possible to use it, and they are on the inside — requires immersion (so it appears from Beit Yosef in the name of Hagahot Maimoniyot chapter 17).}
mechaber.8#main: One who borrows or rents a vessel from a non-Jew does not require immersion; but if a Jew bought it from the non-Jew and lent it to his fellow — it requires immersion, for it was already obligated in the hands of the first; and some say that if the first did not take it for the purpose of a meal but to cut cards and the like — he need not immerse it: {Rama: But the first is forbidden to use it for meal purposes even casually without immersion, even though he took it to cut cards (logical opinion and Orach Chaim); and likewise if the second Jew bought it from the first for meal purposes — the second requires immersion (Beit Yosef).}
mechaber.9#main: If a non-Jew pawned a vessel to a Jew — if it appears from the mind of the non-Jew that he wishes to sink it in his possession, it requires immersion; and if not — he immerses it without a blessing, or buys another vessel and immerses it with it: (and if in the end it sank in his possession, he returns and immerses it without a blessing) (Beit Yosef in the name of an Ashkenazi responsum and Agur, and it is in the responsum of Maharil siman 60).
mechaber.10#main: A Jew who gave money to a non-Jewish craftsman to make a vessel for him from it does not require immersion (so it appears from Mordechai): {Rama: And some disagree (Tur in the name of Ritzba) and one should immerse it without a blessing; and if some of the money from which the vessel was made belongs to the non-Jew — it requires immersion (it appears from Mordechai); and likewise a Jewish craftsman who made a vessel for a non-Jew and bought it from him — he immerses it likewise without a blessing if the non-Jew gave all the metals (Arukh); but if he made it for himself and only bought the metals from the non-Jew, or gave some metals of his own — he does not require immersion (Beit Yosef in the name of Hagahot Ashiri).}
mechaber.11#main: A Jew who sold a vessel to a non-Jew and returned and bought it from him requires immersion; but if he pawned it in his possession and returned and redeemed it from him — he does not require immersion: {Rama: A Jew and a non-Jew who bought a vessel in partnership do not require immersion; a Jew from whom they were stolen or robbed and his vessels were returned to him — he does not require immersion; but a minister or governor who forced a Jew and took his vessels and they were returned to him — they require immersion, for they already sank in the possession of the non-Jew (Arukh).}
mechaber.12#main: One must immerse the handles of the vessel.
mechaber.13#main: One must remove rust before immersion; and if he did not remove it — if he is particular about it, it is a chatzitzah; and if he scraped and put it in coals and a little rust still remains that cannot be removed — through this it is its minority that he is not particular about, and it is not a chatzitzah (and see above siman 202 regarding the law of chatzitzah).
mechaber.14#main: We do not rely on a minor regarding immersion of vessels. (But if he immersed before an adult — it is a valid immersion) (Terumat HaDeshen siman 257).
mechaber.15#main: If one immersed vessels through a non-Jew — their immersion is valid. (But he is not believed regarding the immersion) (logical opinion).
mechaber.16#main: If he forgot and did not immerse a vessel before Shabbat or before Yom Tov — he gives it to a non-Jew as a gift and afterward borrows it from him, and it is permitted to use it: {Rama: And so he should do even on a weekday in a place where he has no mikveh (Beit Yosef); and if he transgressed and used the vessel without immersion — what he used is not forbidden, and he immerses it again (Tur and the poskim).}

mechaber.1#main: The signs of eggs and their laws. In it are 10 seifim: Signs of eggs to recognize that they are from a pure fowl — if both ends are rounded or pointed, or if the white was outside and the yolk inside — it is known that it is an egg of an impure fowl; and even if the seller says they are from a pure fowl, we do not rely on him. And if one end is round and spherical and the other end pointed and spherical, and the white is outside and the yolk inside — it is possible that it is an egg of an impure fowl and possible that it is an egg of a pure fowl; therefore one asks the hunter — a Jew (or a gentile) (Tur and Beit Yosef in name of Hagahot Maimoniyot and so too in name of R' Yitzchak ibn Chaviv) — the seller: if he told him it is from such-and-such fowl and we recognize that that fowl is pure — we rely on him; and if he said from a pure fowl and did not state its name — we do not rely on him; therefore one does not buy eggs from gentiles unless he recognized them and has in them a recognizable familiarity that they are eggs of such-and-such pure fowl; and we are not concerned lest they are eggs of a treifah or nevelah.
mechaber.2#main: Now the custom is to buy eggs indiscriminately from anyone, because eggs of impure fowl are not found among us: {Rama: And specifically with common eggs — meaning chicken eggs or goose eggs and the like; but one does not buy eggs from fowl that are not common more than from impure fowl until he sees the signs as explained (Arukh general rule 42).}
mechaber.3#main: An egg of nevelah and treifah — even if it was completed such that similar ones are sold in the market — is forbidden; and even if it was mixed into a thousand, all are forbidden; but a doubt whether it is an egg of nevelah or an egg of a slaughtered animal — it is permitted even without a mixture; but a doubt whether it is an egg of treifah or an egg of a slaughtered animal — it is forbidden: {Rama: And if the chicken was slaughtered and found treifah — the law of eggs is like the law of milk that was milked from an animal (Beit Yosef); and see above siman 81.}
mechaber.4#main: If one struck a chicken on its tail and it laid its egg before it was completed — it is permitted, and there is no concern here for eiver min ha'chai; provided it is not entangled in sinews.
mechaber.5#main: An egg of impure fowl that was cooked with others — if it is in its shell it does not forbid; and if it is peeled it forbids (and if it is pierced its law is like peeled) (Arukh general rule 42 and hagahah ShaDa); and one needs sixty-one permitted eggs corresponding to it to nullify it (and even if it is not whole but only broken) (in Arukh and Beit Yosef in name of Rashba); and if it was cooked in a permitted dish one needs only sixty of the dish to nullify it; and an egg that has a chick or blood forbids what is cooked with it even if it is not peeled: {Rama: And shells of prohibition combine also with permission to nullify the prohibition, and all the more shells of permission (Tosafot Nedarim 15 and Yerushalmi and Bavli — see s.k. 14); and see above siman 99.}
mechaber.6#main: An egg of treifah and nevelah — its law is like the law of an egg of impure fowl, that whatever is not peeled and was cooked with others does not forbid, for it is merely like water; {Rama: And some say all eggs have the same law and forbid even when not peeled (Tur in name of Beit HaTaharah and majority of poskim); and so one should practice where there is no great loss; but where there is great loss one may rely on the lenient.}
mechaber.7#main: A chick born from an egg of nevelah and treifah — permitted: {Rama: And some say we do not practice so (in Arukh); and l'chatchila one should be careful.}
mechaber.8#main: An egg of impure fowl in which the fowl began to form — they would flog because of sheretz of the fowl; and an egg of pure fowl in which the fowl began to form and she ate it — they would prepare for it a blow of rebelliousness.
mechaber.9#main: A treifah does not give birth; therefore a fowl that is a safek treifah and laid eggs — one waits with it until it lays all its eggs that it already claims; if it will lay again — it is kosher, and we know this when it paused between the end of one laying and the beginning of another a full twenty-one days, for such is its gestation period; and the same law for a chicken that never laid, born with a safek of treifot — that if it lays after twenty-one days from when it was born it is a safek treifah and the eggs are permitted (Orach Chaim brings it Beit Yosef end siman 57).
mechaber.10#main: One does not sell an egg of nevelah and treifah to a gentile lest he return and sell it to a Jew. How should he act? He breaks it in a bowl and sells it to a gentile — for then certainly a Jew will not buy it from him. In what case is this said — when we see it broken in his hand that there is concern a Jew sold it to him because it is treifah; but it is permitted to buy from him bread kneaded with eggs in a place where they are accustomed to eat bread of gentiles, since the broken egg is not seen in his hand: {Rama: And some say that now that we are not careful about bread of gentiles, one should not sell a forbidden egg to a gentile even broken, lest he mix it with bread and sell it to a Jew (Arukh general rule 42 and Mordechai in name of Semak); and so is the custom in a place where they make bread with eggs and practice leniency to buy it; but in other places there is no concern.}

mechaber.1#main: Not to eat cheese after meat. In it are 4 seifim: One who ate meat — even of wild animal and fowl — may not eat cheese afterward until he waits six hours; and even if he waited the measure — if there is meat between the teeth he must remove it; and one who nurses a baby must wait: {Rama: And if he afterward finds meat between the teeth and removes it — he must rinse his mouth before eating cheese (Ran chapter 25). And some say one need not wait six hours but immediately if he cleared the table and recited Birkat HaMazon he is permitted through wiping and rinsing (Tosafot and Mordechai chapter 25 and Hagahot Ashiri and Hagahot Maimoniyot chapter 9 Laws of Forbidden Foods and Ra'avyah); and the simple custom in these lands is to wait one hour after eating meat and then eat cheese; however they must also recite Birkat HaMazon after meat (per Arukh and hagahah ShaDa) — for then it is like another meal and permitted to eat per the lenient; but without Birkat HaMazon waiting an hour does not help, and there is no difference whether one waited the hour before or after Birkat HaMazon (logical opinion from Maharai and unlike Orach Chaim); and if he finds meat between his teeth after the hour he must pick and remove it (logical opinion from implication of Ran above); and some say one should not recite Birkat HaMazon intending to eat cheese (Arukh in name of Maharach); but we are not careful about this and some are meticulous to wait six hours after eating meat for cheese — and so is correct to do.}
mechaber.2#main: One who ate cheese is permitted to eat meat immediately afterward, provided he examines his hands that nothing of cheese sticks to them; and if it is night and he cannot examine them well — he must wash them; and he must wipe his mouth and rinse it; and wiping is that he chews bread and wipes his mouth well with it; and so with anything he wishes except groats and dates and vegetables, because they stick in the crevices (meaning a place above the esophagus near the teeth) and do not wipe well; and afterward he rinses his mouth with water or wine. In what case is this said — with meat of domestic animal and wild animal; but if he comes to eat fowl meat after cheese he needs neither wiping nor rinsing: {Rama: And some are stringent even with other meat after cheese (Mordechai in name of Maharam and Beit Yosef in Orach Chaim siman 173); and so is the custom — that whenever the cheese is hard one does not eat afterward even fowl meat, as with cheese after meat (and so in Zohar); and some are lenient and one should not protest, only that they do wiping, rinsing, and netilat yadayim; however it is good to be stringent.}
mechaber.3#main: One who ate a meat dish is permitted to eat afterward a cheese dish, and rinsing between them is only optional (and some require rinsing) (Sha'arim and hagahah ShaDa); but if he comes to eat the cheese itself after a meat dish, or the meat itself after a cheese dish — he must wash his hands: {Rama: And fat of meat has the law of meat itself (Rashba siman 310 and Mordechai and hagahah ShaDa); and now the custom is to be stringent not to eat cheese after a meat dish as after meat itself, and one should not change and breach the fence (Arukh and Beit Yosef); however if there is no meat in the dish only that it was cooked in a meat pot — permitted to eat cheese afterward (there) and there is no custom to be stringent; and so the custom is to eat meat after a dish that has cheese or milk; however one should wash hands between them, even if he will not eat actual meat but only a meat dish after a cheese dish if he touched them with his hands (in Sha'arim and hagahah Shaarei Dura); a waiter who serves at a meal and touches food does not need rinsing, for they required rinsing only for eaters (Beit Yosef in name of Rashi).}
mechaber.4#main: One who ate cheese and wants to eat meat must clear from the table the crumbs of bread they ate with the cheese; and it is forbidden to eat cheese on a cloth on which they ate meat (and likewise the reverse is forbidden) (as appears in Arukh); and all the more it is forbidden to cut cheese, even cold, with a knife they regularly use for meat; and not only that but even the bread they eat with cheese is forbidden to cut with the knife used for cutting meat: {Rama: And likewise the reverse is forbidden; however through sticking in hard ground it is permitted (Beit Yosef in name of Orach Chaim and Kol Bo); but already all Israel practice having two knives and marking one of them so it has a recognizable sign, and they practice marking the dairy one — and one should not change the custom of Israel.}

mechaber.1#main: In which meat does the law of basar b'chalav apply and how is cooking called. In it are 11 seifim: It is written in the Torah 'You shall not cook a kid in its mother's milk' three times — one for prohibition of cooking, one for prohibition of eating, and one for prohibition of benefit; and it derived eating in the language of cooking to say that it is not forbidden from the Torah except by way of cooking; but rabbinically it is forbidden in every manner (all basar b'chalav that is not forbidden from the Torah is permitted for benefit (Tur and Arukh general rule 40)).
mechaber.2#main: A kid is not specific — the same law applies to ox, sheep, and goat; and it makes no difference whether in milk of its own species or in milk of another species, only that Scripture spoke in the present tense.
mechaber.3#main: It applies only to meat of a pure domestic animal in milk of a pure domestic animal; but pure meat in impure milk or impure meat in pure milk is permitted in cooking and benefit; and meat of wild animal and fowl — even in pure milk — is permitted in cooking and benefit, and even for eating it is forbidden only rabbinically; but fish and locusts have no prohibition even rabbinically: {Rama: And the custom is to make almond milk and place fowl meat in it, since it is only rabbinic; but meat of domestic animal one should not place near almond milk because of marit ayin, as explained above siman 66 regarding blood (logical opinion).}
mechaber.4#main: It is forbidden to cook in a woman's milk because of marit ayin; and if it fell into the dish it is nullified and no measure is required: {Rama: And it appears accordingly that all the more so it is forbidden l'chatchila to cook in impure milk or impure meat in pure milk (logical opinion); and specifically meat of domestic animal, but for fowl which is rabbinic there is no concern.}
mechaber.5#main: Eggs found in fowl — if they are complete, meaning they have white and yolk — even though entangled in sinews, behold it is complete and permitted to eat it with milk; but if it has only yolk — forbidden to cook them in milk; but if one ate them by themselves — permitted to eat cheese or milk afterward.
mechaber.6#main: Smoked meat and meat cooked in Tiberias hot springs — one is not flogged for it; and likewise one who cooks meat in milk-water or in milk of a dead animal or male animal, or who cooked blood in milk — is exempt and one is not flogged for eating it because of basar b'chalav: {Rama: And male milk is not called milk at all; and if it fell into a meat pot it does not forbid; but milk of a dead animal and milk-water forbid the food like milk itself, and even for cooking there is room to forbid l'chatchila (so appears in Arukh general rule 41); and some say forbidden to stoke fire under a gentile's pot because they sometimes cook milk sometimes meat and stoking under their pot leads to cooking meat in milk (hagahah Mordechai chapter Kol HaTzlamim); they also wrote one should not mix water used to rinse meat vessels with water used to rinse milk vessels and give before an animal, for they are forbidden for benefit (Mahariu); they also wrote the vessel used for head-washing water — one should not use it, for they make it from ashes on the stove and it is customary for meat and milk to mix there (Maharil); therefore one should forbid using winter-house oven pots because meat and milk sometimes splash on them from pots cooking in ovens (Mahariu); and b'dieved one need not be concerned in all this; and even l'chatchila this is only a general stringency and one who is lenient has not lost.}
mechaber.7#main: One who cooks placenta in milk is liable; and likewise one who eats it; but one who cooks placenta-sheath, or skin, sinews, bones, horn cores, and soft hooves — is exempt; and likewise one who eats them is exempt.
mechaber.8#main: There are those who say that whey of milk (meaning milk extracted when cheese coagulates) is not included in milk-water and is forbidden from the Torah; but milk-water means after they make cheese they cook the whey and the food floats on top and only water remains — this is called milk-water.
mechaber.9#main: Milk found in the stomach is not milk and is permitted to cook meat in it, even in the clear part therein (Tur in name of Rif and Rambam); and some forbid (Tosafot and Rosh and Rabbenu Tam and Rashba and Ran) (and so is the custom).
mechaber.10#main: Milk found in the stomach (l'chatchila one should not place it in the stomach until the milk congeals inside the stomach (Arukh general rule 18 in name of R' Simchah and hagahah Ashiri); but b'dieved one need not be concerned until) that was salted in its stomach or stood in it one day — (then) forbidden to use for rennet: {Rama: And if one used it for rennet — if it is the clear part it forbids all the cheeses until there is sixty in the milk used for rennet against the forbidden stomach; and if there was sixty in the milk all is permitted; and if the stomach was dry it forbids nothing even if there was not sixty in the milk against the stomach (per Rabbenu Tam); and if the stomach was clear from the start and became hard it has the law of clear (Beit Yosef in name of Rashba and poskim); and some are lenient (ShaDa and Beit Yosef in name of Mordechai); and where there is loss one may be lenient; stomach skin — sometimes they salt it and dry it until it becomes like wood and fill it with milk — permitted, for after it dried it is merely like wood and has no meat moisture (Beit Yosef in name of Shibolei Leket).}
mechaber.11#main: If one set cheese in the skin of a kosher stomach — it has taste of forbidden meat; and if not — it is permitted; but one who sets in the skin of nevelah, treifah, or impure animal — forbids in any amount: {Rama: Because it is a forbidden item in itself and setting even in a thousand is not nullified (so Beit Yosef per Rashba and Ran); and specifically when there was no other rennet there only the forbidden; but if there was also permitted rennet — it is this-and-this causes and permitted if there is sixty against the forbidden (from implication of Mordechai).}

mechaber.1#main: The laws of udder (kachal). In it are 4 seifim: Udder is forbidden by rabbinic decree, for there is no meat cooked in milk that is forbidden from the Torah; therefore if one tore it and rinsed the milk in it — it is permitted to roast and eat it; and if one tore it in two directions and smeared it on the wall until no moisture of milk remained — it is permitted to cook it with meat; and udder that was not torn — whether of a young animal that did not nurse or of an adult — is forbidden to cook; and if one transgressed and cooked it — if by itself (and all the more if roasted) it is permitted to eat it; and if he cooked it with other meat — one estimates it with sixty and the udder is counted in the number: How so? If everything with the udder was as sixty in the udder — the udder is forbidden and the rest permitted; and if there was less than sixty — all is forbidden; in any case if it fell into another pot it forbids that pot, and one estimates with sixty as at first, for the udder itself that was cooked becomes like the forbidden piece, and one estimates it only as it is at the time it was cooked, not as it was when it fell: {Rama: And some say if it fell first into a pot that does not have sixty and became forbidden — if it then fell into another pot the udder does not combine for sixty (Tur in name of Rashba and logical opinion for Ran unlike Beit Yosef for Ran); and so is primary.}
mechaber.2#main: The custom is not to cook it with meat at all, and to cook it without meat — in a pan or pastry requires tearing in two directions and smearing on the wall; and for roasting — tearing in two directions: {Rama: And if one transgressed and cooked it — if torn in two directions and smeared on the wall, there is room to permit b'dieved (Sefer HaTerumah and Mordechai and Hagahot Maimoniyot and Tur and per Avodat HaTaharah) where there is great loss; but otherwise one should not permit; and that the custom is to tear it and cut it many times in two directions over its entire surface is preferable and more effective than smearing on the wall (Terumat HaDeshen siman 182); and for roasting the custom is l'chatchila to tear it in two directions and smear on the wall (Arukh general rule 18); however if one transgressed and roasted it even without tearing it is permitted if roasted alone without meat with it (Hagahot Maimoniyot and ShaDa and Tur and per Avodat HaTaharah); and if roasted with meat with it — if torn in two directions and smeared on the wall, both are permitted; and if not — the upper is permitted and the lower forbidden (Beit Yosef in name of Tosafot and Rosh and Mordechai and Arukh); and one should not forbid both lest the spit was turned over, for b'dieved we do not establish prohibition (Orach Chaim); but l'chatchila one should not roast it with meat at all; and for a pot without meat the custom is to forbid it l'chatchila (Rashi and poskim); and the same for frying even without meat (Beit Yosef); and even if the udder dried out (Orach Chaim); and if one transgressed and cooked it in a pot alone — b'dieved permitted if torn in two directions and smeared on the wall (Rashi and Ra'avad and ShaDa and Mordechai and per Avodat HaTaharah); however if it dried out — meaning after thirty days — if one transgressed and cooked it even with meat — b'dieved permitted (ShaDa and hagahah and R' Yechiel); and to make pastry from udder without meat the custom permits if they do not bake the pastry on a griddle; but on a griddle its law is like cooking in a pot (Maharai in hagahah and Arukh general rule 18); and some commentators are stringent in every pastry if the udder was not dried first. Some are stringent not to bake udder pastry with meat pastry in a small oven — only one should be placed at the mouth of the oven; and it is good to be careful l'chatchila even though it is only a general stringency (Beit Yosef and Arukh).}
mechaber.3#main: It is permitted to cut hot udder with a knife used to cut meat (and all the more raw udder even though it is full of milk) (Tosafot Nedarim 51); and likewise permitted to cut meat with a knife used for udder; and the same law to eat this in a vessel in which that was eaten: {Rama: And the same to roast this on a spit on which that was roasted; and the same law permitted to place it in a bowl with roasted meat even if both are hot; for after roasting udder its law is like other meat for everything (Beit Yosef in name of Rashba and Arukh); and specifically if it was roasted properly — meaning they tore it first in two directions and smeared on the wall; but if one transgressed and roasted without tearing or with slight tearing — all these matters are forbidden l'chatchila (Tur and Beit Yosef) and b'dieved all is permitted; and if they tore properly and roasted and afterward found pockets full of milk — no concern (Arukh chapter 11); and likewise if they left it whole with its milk a full day before roasting — permitted (there); and we do not say kavush k'mevushal in such a case (there).}
mechaber.4#main: To roast udder or to salt it with meat — its law is like the law of roasting or salting liver with meat; and some permit salting udder on meat: {Rama: And one should not salt it with meat; but b'dieved in every matter it is permitted (Arukh general rule 18); stomach skin after its milk was removed from inside and rinsed has the law of other meat and is permitted to salt it with other meat and has no law of udder at all (there).}

mechaber.1#main: Fish and egg cooked in a meat pot — whether permitted to eat with cheese. In it are 7 seifim: Fish that were cooked or roasted in a meat pot that is well washed so that there is no clinging fat on it — permitted to eat them with kutach, because it is noten ta'am bar noten ta'am of heter; and if it was not well washed — if on the surface of the pot there is more than one part in sixty in the fish, forbidden to eat them with kutach.
mechaber.2#main: An egg that was cooked in water in a dairy pot — permitted to place it inside poultry, even l'chatchila; but if it was cooked in a pot with meat — even in its shell — forbidden to eat it with kutach: {Rama: And some are stringent with roasting and cooking to forbid noten ta'am bar noten ta'am (Ribban in name of Rashi and Arukh general rule 34 — Mordechai brought it and Or Zarua); and the custom is to forbid l'chatchila; and b'dieved permitted in every case (Arukh); and specifically to eat with milk and the meat itself; but to place them in their vessels — permitted l'chatchila (Issur veHeter HaArukh); and so they practiced; and likewise if they did not cook or roast at first but only came up in a meat vessel — permitted to eat them with milk itself and likewise the reverse (his own reasoning); and likewise if the vessel in which they were cooked or roasted was for spoilage such that it was not ben yomo, they practice permissibility l'chatchila to eat them with the other species (there in Arukh); and all this when the food is not a sharp item; but if it was a sharp item, such as if they cooked sharp things in a meat vessel — even if it is not ben yomo, or if they ground spices in a meat mortar — if they ate it with milk it forbids even b'dieved until there is sixty against the meat absorbed in them (Arukh general rule 24, and so appears in responsum of Rashba siman 249 and Beit Yosef siman 96 in name of Semak and Hagahot ShaDa siman 62 in name of Maharash and Agur in name of Mordechai); and nevertheless a sharp food item is not called such on account of a small amount of spice in it, only if the whole thing is a sharp item and the majority is like its entirety; and see above siman 96.}
mechaber.3#main: Meat bowls that were rinsed in a dairy cauldron in hot water that yad soledes bo applies to them — even if both are ben yomo — permitted, because it is noten ta'am bar noten ta'am of heter; and this is when he says it is clear to me that there was no clinging fat on them; and if there was clinging fat on them — there must be in the water sixty corresponding to the substance of the fat on the surface of the bowl: {Rama: And some forbid even if there is no clinging fat on them (Tur in name of Semak and Semag and Semak and ShaDa and Rif and Tosafot and Mordechai and Ran and Hagahot Maimoniyot and Piskei Maharai and Orach Chaim) unless one of the vessels is not ben yomo from absorption of a kli rishon; and then all the vessels are permitted; and the water is treated with prohibition l'chatchila; but if both are ben yomo and he rinsed them together in a kli rishon — all is forbidden; and so they practice and one should not change; and specifically when they were rinsed together and in a kli rishon; but if they were rinsed one after the other, or in a kli sheni — even together — all is permitted (Arukh general rule 34); and if he poured from a kli rishon of meat onto a dairy vessel — its law is like a kli rishon and it forbids if it was ben yomo; but if he poured boiling water that is neither of meat nor of milk onto meat and dairy vessels together — even if clinging fat is on them — all is permitted, for pouring is not literally like a kli rishon such that the vessels onto which he pours will absorb one from the other (there). And if a dairy bowl is found among meat vessels — we are not concerned lest they were rinsed together in the manner that is forbidden (Hagahot ShaDa and Orach Chaim).}
mechaber.4#main: It appears to me that if they put ash in the hot water in the cauldron before placing the pots in it — even though clinging fat is on them — it is permitted, for through the ash it is noten ta'am lefegem.
mechaber.5#main: One does not place a vessel that has kutach next to a vessel that has salt; but it is permitted to place it next to a vessel that has vinegar: {Rama: And specifically if the vessels are uncovered; and even so, if he transgressed and placed them together it is permitted and we are not concerned lest something fell into the salt (Hagahot ShaDa and Arukh).}
mechaber.6#main: It is permitted to place inside a chest a meat bowl next to a dairy bowl: {Rama: And some are stringent l'chatchila (Hagahot Ashiri in name of Or Zarua); and it is good to be careful l'chatchila where it is not needed.}
mechaber.7#main: Salt placed in a meat bowl is permitted to place it in milk: {Rama: And one who is stringent also in this — blessing shall come upon him, for some are stringent l'chatchila (Tosafot and Semag and Orach Chaim).}
